Bi OM iNeralizati ON Ba Sic S Understanding the fundamentals of coral calcification (i.e., the processes involved in the nucleation and growth of aragonite crystals) is a crucial first step in predicting the response of corals and coral reef ecosystems to future climate change, including ocean acidification. A useful place to start thinking about calcification strategies in the marine environment is to recognize that all marine calcifiers, including the reef-building or “stony” corals, have to overcome the kinetic barriers to CaCO3 precipitation that exist naturally in seawater. Today, the surface ocean is supersaturated with respect to CaCO3, which means that there are more than enough calcium and carbonate ions in solution to enable CaCO3 to precipitate out. The saturation state of seawater with respect to aragonite, the form of calcium carbonate that corals produce, is denoted by the symbol Ωar.

It is defined as the product of the actual measured concentrations of calcium and carbonate ions dissolved in seawater divided by the product of the concentrations of calcium and carbonate ions when they are saturated (at equilibrium) in seawater, as follows: Ωar = [Ca2+] x [CO3 2–] / [Ca2+] x [CO3 2–]sat. Because the calcium ion concentration [Ca2+] in seawater is very high and relatively constant, variations in Ωar are determined mainly by the carbonate ion concentration [CO3 2–]. Today, the [CO3 2–] of seawater in the low-latitude surface ocean is about 250 µmol kg-1. Aragonite saturation is reached at a [CO3 2–] of about 60 µmol kg-1. Thus, the tropical surface ocean is, in general, but with notable exceptions such as the eastern tropical Pacific, about four times supersaturated with respect to aragonite. When Ωar > 1 (i.e., [CO3 2–] > 60 µmol kg-1), aragonite should, theoretically, precipitate from seawater. Conversely, when Ωar < 1, aragonite should dissolve in seawater. The warm tropical ocean where most coral reefs are found is highly supersaturated with respect to aragonite, in other words, Ωar can be significantly greater than 1. Nevertheless, neither calcite nor aragonite will form spontaneously because there are kinetic barriers that prevent nucleation and/or crystal growth. These kinetic barriers include the high hydration energy of the calcium ions (e.g., Lippmann, 1973), the low concentration and activity of the carbonate ions (e.g., Garrels and Thompson, 1962; Lippmann, 1973), and the presence of high concentrations of sulfate and magnesium (e.g., Usdowski, 1968; Kastner, 1984).

Most marine calcifiers, therefore, must nucleate and grow CaCO3 crystals within compartments that are isolated or semi-isolated from the external seawater, and within which they can modify, regulate, and control conditions, including several meters in height. Countless skeletons accreted over many millennia provide the reef framework, the concrete jungles of the tropical ocean that provide myriad marine and terrestrial species with habitat, nesting grounds, and food. For human populations along tropical coastlines, healthy reefs provide natural buffers to beach erosion, barriers to tsunamis and hurricanes, and significant income through tourism and fisheries. By one estimate, the net global economic value of coral reefs worldwide is a staggering $29.8 billion each year (Cesar et al., 2003). Over the next century, rising levels of atmospheric CO2 will increase the concentration of total dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) in seawater, but simultaneously reduce seawater pH and the abundance of carbonate ions [CO3 2–] that corals and other marine calcifiers use to build their skeletons. For this reason, there is growing concern that the so-called “acidification” of the surface ocean may slow rates of CaCO3 production or “calcification” by reef-building corals to a point where rates of reef erosion exceed rates of skeletal accretion, leading to the gradual, worldwide loss of coral reef ecosystems as we know them.

Data from a wide range of laboratory experiments have fueled this concern, demonstrating that coral calcification (skeleton-building) can be highly sensitive to changes in seawater carbonate ion concentration. In this paper, we show how this process might work using a model based on the behavior of nonbiological (abiogenic) aragonites when grown in increasingly “acidified” seawater. We show that coral calcification under any circumstances is energetically costly to the coral animal and that the energy Oceanography Vol.22, No.4120 in some cases the carbonate chemistry of the calcifying fluid, to enable CaCO3 precipitation to occur. Coccolithophores and gorgonians, for example, produce calcite and high-magnesium calcite intracellularly, the marine alga Halimeda accretes aggregations of acicular aragonite needles extracellularly within spaces created between cell membranes, and corals and mollusks accrete their CaCO3 crystals within compartments created between the tissue and the existing skeleton or shell. In addition, there is substantial evidence for the involvement of organic molecules in the biomineralization processes of many marine calcifiers. Organic molecules may play a role in reducing the surface free energy required for nucleation (e.g., Teng et al., 1998), in guiding site-specific nucleation that results in species-specific skeletal architectures, or in buffering the pH of the calcifying fluid against large fluctuations in internal CO2 concentrations caused by cycles in photosynthesis and respiration (Holcomb et al., 2009).

In stony corals, skeletal formation is entirely external to the organism (extracellular) but the skeleton is not exposed to seawater. Corals either sit on top of or wrap themselves around their skeletons (Figure 1A) and the skeletal surface is completely enveloped by tissue, separated from the external seawater environment by four layers of cells. Kinetic inhibition of aragonite nucleation and growth has to be overcome, and there are several ways this could be accomplished by the coral. The exact mechanisms involved have important implications for understanding and predicting the impact of ocean climate changes on coral; however, opportunities for scientists to directly observe or monitor the site of calcification in corals have been limited because of its small size and inaccessible location beneath the tissue. One approach that has proven fruitful is to compare the composition and morphology of coral aragonites with abiogenic aragonites precipitated experimentally from highly supersaturated seawater solution in a laboratory beaker (e.g., Gaetani and Cohen, 2003; Holcomb et al., 2009). Figure 1B–D shows the morphology and microstructural arrangement of crystals in a coral skeleton. All the different components of the skeleton seen in Figure 1A are built of bundles of fine, needle-shaped crystals that are several microns in length (f in Figure 1B and Figure 1D) and that radiate from discrete aggregations of tiny granular crystals, each several nanometers in diameter (g in Figure 1B, and Figure 1C). In many corals, there is a distinct diurnal cycle to the formation of these crystals: the granular crystals form at night, whereas the needle-shaped crystals form during the day (Holcomb, 2009).

Each aggregate of granular crystals and its associated bundle of needles is called a sclerodermite (Wells, 1956). Sclerodermites are the basic building blocks or “bricks” of the coral skeleton. Aragonite crystals precipitated in the laboratory from a highly supersaturated seawater solution in the absence of a coral (i.e., abiogenic aragonites) bear remarkable resemblance to the coral sclerodermites (Figure 2). Nucleation, which occurs at very high aragonite saturation states (Ωar > 20), produces aggregates of submicron-sized granular crystals. At lower aragonite saturation states (Ωar ~ 6–19), crystal growth is favored over nucleation. The growth phase produces bundles of fine, needleshaped crystals. Each aggregate of granular crystals and its associated needle-shaped crystals is called a “spherulite” (Figure 2B; Holcomb et al., 2009). Aragonitic spherulites precipitated from a supersaturated seawater solution are compositionally (i.e., chemically) and morphologically similar to coral “sclerodermites, ” as evident in Figure 2. Based on this similarity, it is feasible that one mechanism corals may employ to achieve aragonite nucleation and growth is by elevating the saturation state of seawater trapped in an isolated or semiisolated calcifying compartment (Cohen and McConnaughey, 2003). Abiogenic aragonites grown experimentally from seawater over a range of aragonite saturation states show systemmatic and progressive changes in crystal morphology caused by changes in crystal growth rate (Figure 3).

Crystals grown experimentally at relatively low aragonite saturation states (Ωar ~ 6) are short, wide, and highly faceted, consistent with low crystal growth rates (e.g., Lofgren, 1974, 1981; Figure 3C). When the saturation state of the experimental seawater is increased during growth, the crystals produced are longer and thinner, more bladelike in appearance, and less faceted, consistent with a progressive increase in crystal growth rate (Figure 3A,B). This change in crystal morphology with increasing seawater saturation state can be quantified using the crystal aspect ratio or the ratio of its length to its width. In Figure 3D, the aspect ratio of aragonite crystals grown under experimental conditions is plotted against the saturation state of the seawater in which they grew. The crystal aspect ratio is linearly related to aragonite saturation state. The lower the seawater saturation state, the lower the crystal growth rate, and thus the lower the crystal aspect ratio. The relationship between seawater saturation state and crystal aspect ratio in these experiments can be described by the following equation: Ωar = 0.93 (± 0.06) x crystal aspect ratio (µm) + 0.20(± 0.89); r2 = 0.94. Al-Horani et al. (2003) placed micro-pH electrodes within the calcifying space of the zooxanthellate coral Galaxea fascicularis while manipulating light levels in the laboratory. The pH of the fluid within the coral’s calcifying compartment cycle from ambient seawater values (~ 8.2) in the dark to values significantly elevated above ambient (> 9.0) in the light, when most of the calcification occurs. This rise in pH translates to an increase in the aragonite saturation state of the calcifying fluid that is significantly above that of the ambient seawater, potentially five to 10 times higher depending on DIC concentration.

Al-Horani et al. (2003) also reported a small increase, ~ 10% above ambient, in the concentration of calcium ions at the calcifying site. Indeed, if Al-Horani et al. ’s (2003) unique timeseries data of pH changes at the site of calcification reflect actual conditions and changes within the calcifying space over the diurnal cycle, then the saturation state of the calcifying fluid ramps up immediately following daybreak. How is this achieved? Cohen and McConnaughy (2003) proposed that rapid and effective elevation of calcifying fluid pH and saturation state could be achieved with a plasma membrane Ca2+-ATPase acting as a Ca2+/H+ exchanger (or antiporter), which removes two H+ ions from the calcifying fluid for every Ca2+ ion transported from the calicoblastic epithelial cells into the calcifying space. Subsequent work by Zoccola et al. (2004) lends some support to this model, showing that Ca2+-ATPase expression is highly concentrated in the calicoblastic epithelial cells that overly the coral skeleton and are presumed to be involved in calcification. The potential role of Ca2+-ATPase, proton pumps and other enzymes in coral calcification highlights the energetic cost to the coral of producing aragonite crystals to build a skeleton. Under the Cohen and McConnaughey (2003) model, every µmol of CaCO3 produced by the coral requires the removal of two µmol protons (H+ ions) from the calcifying fluid, and the expenditure of 1 µmol of “energy” or ATP . For a coral producing 3.7 µmol CaCO3 per hour and respiring at a rate of 3.1 µmol CO2 per hour (e.g., Dennison and Barnes, 1988), and assuming 6 mol ATP per mol CO2 produced, calcification may consume up to 20% of the coral’s energy budget. When the energy required to produce organic matrix proteins that constitute 0.1–1% of the coral skeleton is included, up to 30% of the coral’s energy budget may be devoted to calcification (Allemand et al., in press). Although these estimates of the energetic cost of calcification are preliminary, it is clear from studies of corals reared under fed and starved conditions (e.g., Houlbreque et al., 2008) that calcification is an active, physiological process that requires significant amounts of energy to drive it.

However, the skeleton accreted under these conditions was far from healthy, and SEM images of the aragonite crystals revealed that their morphology, organization, and packing is very different from those accreted by corals under ambient CO2 conditions. Figure 5 illustrates progressive changes in coral crystal morphology as a function of seawater saturation state in the experimental aquaria. Aragonite crystals accreted by corals reared under ambient CO2 are similar to those found in coral skeletons collected in the field: acicular in shape, several µm in length, 0.5–1 µm wide, tightly packed into discrete bundles, and oriented with their c-axes aligned or in parallel with adjacent crystals in the bundle (Figure 5A). Crystals in coral skeletons accreted in seawater with decreasing saturation states show progressive changes in crystal morphology that are consistent with a slowdown in crystal growth rate (Figure 5B–D). Individual crystals within bundles become increasingly short, fat, and faceted as the saturation state in the aquarium seawater decreases. Near aragonite saturation (Ωar ~ 1), the crystals are no longer organized into discrete, tightly packed bundles, and in the strongly undersaturated treatment (Ωar ~ 0.2), the crystals are no longer oriented with their c-axes in parallel.

In this treatment, crystal growth is so slow that crystal morphology assumes an orthorhombic shape characteristic of aragonite grown slowly at near equilibrium conditions (Figure 5D). Note that the aspect ratio of the crystals decreases as the Ωar of the aquarium seawater decreases. Applying the relationship between crystal aspect ratio and fluid saturation state established for experimental abiogenic aragonites, we can show that the saturation state of the coral’s internal calcifying fluid is maintained significantly above that of the external seawater in all experimental conditions (Figure 5E). However, the saturation state of the coral’s internal calcifying fluid decreases as that of the external seawater decreases. When the Ωar of the external seawater is ~ 3.7 (i.e., at ambient levels), the coral pumps enough protons from the initial calcifying “intake” water to maintain an internal calcifying fluid saturation state significantly higher than it is outside (Ωar ~ 19).

At this level of aragonite supersaturation, crystals growth is very fast, allowing the coral to quickly build a massive and dense skeleton. When the Ωar of the external seawater is ~ 2.4, the coral works to maintain the calcifying fluid Ωar at around 15. At this level of aragonite supersaturation, crystal growth slows enough to cause the rate of skeletal formation to slow down as well.

When the Ωar of the external seawater is ~ 1, the coral works to maintain the calcifying fluid Ωar at ~ 7. At this level of aragonite supersaturation, the rate of crystal growth slows dramatically and building a normal skeleton becomes almost impossible. When reared in strongly undersaturated seawater, the coral is able to maintain the fluid saturation state just above that at which its minute skeleton will dissolve (Ωar ~ 2). Thus, coral calcification declines with declining seawater saturation state because the saturation state of the internal calcifying fluid declines in concert with it. And, as the saturation state of the internal calcifying fluid declines, the rate of CaCO3 crystal growth becomes too slow to sustain growth of a normal skeleton.

If corals grow aragonite from seawater by pumping protons to raise the saturation state within a calcifying compartment, why don’t corals reared under elevated CO2 (ocean acidification) conditions simply pump more protons in an effort to build a normal skeleton? After all, under elevated CO2, there is even more carbon around, in the form of bicarbonate. And, removing protons from the calcifying fluid would turn that excess bicarbonate into even more carbonate Figure 5. in (a) aragonite crystals accreted by corals (shown in Figure 4) reared in seawater with a range of aragonite saturation states, display systematic and progressive changes in crystal morphology (a–d). in (e), these changes can be quantified using the crystal aspect ratio (the ratio of crystal length to width) and used to estimate changes in the saturation state of the coral’s internal calcifying fluid in response to ocean acidification. Scale bars are 1 µm. From Cohen et al., 2009 E Oceanography december 2009 125 ions for calcification. The answer might lie in the fact that calcification is energetically costly and the coral’s energy budget is not that flexible. A coral building a normal skeleton under elevated CO2 conditions would have to divert more energy to pumping protons from the calcifying fluid than a coral building a normal skeleton under ambient CO2 conditions.

For example, a coral reared in seawater with an aragonite saturation state of ~ 3.7 (pCO2 ~ 400 ppm) would need to remove ~ 4500 nmol protons per ml of fluid to raise the Ωar of the calcifying fluid to 19 (Figure 6). By comparison, a coral reared in seawater with a saturation state of ~ 2.4 (pCO2 ~ 740 ppm) would have to remove > 8000 nmol protons per ml of calcifying fluid to reach Ωar of 19. Conversely, if the energy budget for calcification were fixed and the coral could expend only enough energy to remove 4500 nmol protons from the calcifying fluid independent of the saturation state of the “intake” water, then our calculations show that a coral reared at Ωar ~ 2.4 would be able to elevate the internal saturation state from 2.4 to about 15 (Figure 6). And a coral reared in seawater with Ωar of 1.5 would elevate the internal saturation state to approximately 10 by removing the same number of protons. These numbers are consistent with our estimate of actual calcifying fluid saturation state based on crystal aspect ratios (Figure 5E), and suggest that corals reared under high-CO2 conditions may have worked as hard, and pumped as many protons from their calcifying fluid, as corals in the ambient treatment. However, in our experimental aquaria, there appears to be a limit to the amount of work the corals will do even at the expense of building the healthy skeleton that is so critical to recruitment success.

This result suggests that the coral’s energy budget for calcification might be limited by the availability of nutrients or food. the pO te Ntial rO le OF Nutrie NtS a Nd F OO d iN M Odulati Ng cOral reSpONS e t O Ocea N acidi Ficati ON If it is true that the coral’s energy budget for calcification is limited by the availability of nutrients, then elevating the nutritional status of a coral calcifying in low-saturation-state seawater might provide the additional fuel it needs to maintain healthy calcification rates. This could be done by enhanced heterotrophic feeding or by adding moderate amounts of inorganic nutrients, such as nitrates and phosphates, to stimulate zooxanthellate photosynthesis, providing the coral with carbohydraterich photosynthate to fuel calcification. Normally, nutrient addition stimulates zooxanthellate photosynthesis, which, under ambient CO2 conditions, can lead to CO2 limitation and a decline in calcification (e.g., Marubini and Davies, 1996). However, under elevated CO2 conditions, nutrient addition can support increased zooxanthellate photosynthesis without reducing the total amount of carbon available for calcification. Increased photosynthesis means increased photosynthate and more energy for calcification. Therefore, combining elevated nutrients with elevated CO2 could help to offset the negative impact on calcification of elevated CO2 alone. In at least four separate experiments conducted to date, five different species of coral were reared under significantly elevated CO2 conditions (780–1200 ppm, Ω ~ 1.5–2) with the simultaneous addition of food or inorganic nutrients.

These experimental results are consistent with the earlier findings of Atkinson et al. (1995), which show that nutritionally replete zooxanthellate corals in naturally lowsaturation-state seawaters are capable of accreting skeletons at rates comparable to those achieved by conspecifics in high-saturation-state seawaters. Today, several reefs, including Galàpagos, areas of Pacific Panama, and Jarvis (southern Line Islands), experience levels of aragonite saturation equivalent to that predicted for the open ocean under two times and three times pre-industrial CO2 levels (Manzello et al., 2008; Kathryn Shamberger [PMEL/NOAA] and colleagues, pers.

comm., August 2009). Available data on coral colony growth rates on these reefs, albeit limited, suggest that they are equivalent to and sometimes even rival those of conspecifics in areas where aragonite saturation states are naturally high, such as the western Pacific warm pool. Although no comparative data exist regarding the nutritional status of corals on these high-CO2 reefs, surface ocean nutrient concentrations and rates of primary and secondary production around the islands are significantly elevated compared with oligotrophic reefs. Thus, it appears likely that naturally elevated levels of inorganic nutrients and, consequently, high levels of primary and secondary production, may already be facilitating high coral calcification rates in regions with naturally high dissolved CO2 levels. If, as these experimental and field data suggest, nutrients or food can potentially lessen the severity of the impact of ocean acidification on coral calcification, does this observation change the outlook for corals and coral reefs as the ocean becomes more acidic over this century? The answer is, probably not. Seawater saturation states across the global tropics are predicted to drop to an average of around 2.5–3 by the year 2100 (Feely et al., 2009). However, several models (e.g., Boyd and Doney, 2002) predict that this decline will not be accompanied by an elevation in surface ocean nutrient concentrations, at least in the open ocean.

Enhanced stratification, reduced mixed-layer depth, and slowed circulation caused by greenhouse-gas-induced global warming will likely cause a significant reduction in surface nutrient concentrations across much of the global tropics and subtropics. A recent study showed that spawning female corals are significantly more susceptible to the negative effects of ocean acidification than spawning male corals (Holcomb et al., 2010). The apparent gender discrimination is likely due to the energetically costly process of egg production, leaving little energy available to the coral to temper the effects of acidification on calcification. This example highlights the compounding difficulties that corals will face as they strive to build skeletons in a high-CO2 world. Climate changes that simultaneously reduce the availability of food while making it harder for corals to calcify will impact not only rates of skeletal growth but sexual reproduction, genetic diversity, and rates of recolonization, rendering coral reef ecosystems even more vulnerable to CO2-induced climate changes than they would be to ocean acidification alone.

Mitigation requires identification and prot ection of Areas of Ecological Significance 103 (AES), which have eluded identification at the ocean-basin scale. For this globally significant 104 region, we identify AES using assemblage-level tracking of marine predators and assess current 105 threats and protection levels. Integration of >4000 tracks from 17 bird and mammal species 106 reveal AES around sub-Antarctic islands in the Atlantic and Indian Oceans and over the 107 Antarctic continental shelf. Fishing pressure is disproportionately concentrated inside AES, and 108 climate change over the next century is predicted to impose pressure on these areas, 109 particularly around the Antarctic continent. Currently, 7.1% of the ocean south of 40 ˚S is under 110 formal protection, including 29% of the total AES area. The establishment and regular revision of 111 networks of protection encompassing AES is needed to provide long-term mitigation of growing 112 pressures on Southern Ocean ecosystems. 113 114 The Southern Ocean, defined here as the circumpolar waters south of 40°S, is home to a unique fauna 115 and plays an important role in biogeochemic al cycles and the global climate system 1.

Past industrial 116 sealing, whaling and demersal fishing caused signif icant perturbations from which some Southern 117 Ocean ecosystems are only now starting to recover 3. Squid and toothfish harvesting continue 4,5 and 118 interest in the expansion of Antarctic krill fisheries is growing 6. These target species are important prey 119 for upper trophic organisms with krill a key component of the Southern Ocean food web, raising 120 substantial concerns about impacts on Southern Ocean ecosystems 2. Anthropogenic greenhouse gas 121 emissions are simultaneously causing large changes to the Southern Ocean 7. Strong interest has 122 therefore developed in long-term conservation of the Southern Ocean, but management authorities face 123 the considerable challenge of implementing conservation goals within existing management 124 frameworks2. 125 126 A first step in meeting this challenge is to identify regions that should be considered for protection, for 127 example because of their high biodiversity, biological productivity, or particular importance for life-history 128 stages of species 8,9. The distribution and demography of marine predators provides a viable basis for 129 this10, particularly in the vast and remote Southern Ocean where integrated ecosystem measures are 130 difficult to obtain at management-relevant, ocean-basin scales 11. Indeed, on-shore measures of 131 Southern Ocean marine predators have been used as regional indicators of ecosystem status for 132 several decades12.

Spatial aggregations of predators at sea iden tify not only areas that are important to 133 the predator species themselves, which depend on lower trophic levels 13, but also areas of broader 134 ecosystem importance such as regions of elevated productivity and biomass at lower trophic levels 14. 135 Combining information across predator species with diverse diets and life histories is essential for an 136 ecosystem-wide approach that is less susceptib le to factors affecting individual species 12. Recognition 137 of the value of tracking data for broad-scale conservation decision-making is growing15. 138 139 Using predator tracking data to identify Areas of Ecological Significance 140 In the Southern Ocean, many predator species with differing diets and movement patterns have been 141 tracked16. We synthesised tracking data from 4060 i ndividuals of 17 species (Fig. 1a) to provide a 142 circumpolar assessment of regions of ecological importance in the Southern Ocean. We identified 143 regions preferred by multiple predator species as indi cators of high levels of lower trophic biomass and 144 biodiversity, and refer to these as Areas of Ecological Significance 17 (AES). Our definition of AES is not 145 the same as Ecologically and Biologically Significant Marine Areas (EBSAs), or Key Biodiversity Areas 146 (KBAs). However, it is consistent with severa l of the criteria used for defining EBSAs or KBAs, 147 particularly biological productivity and diversity 8, and so provides a similar qualitative, integrated 148 assessment of biodiversity patterns.

149 150 We assembled tracking data from 17 species of seabirds (12 species) and marine mammals (5 151 species), collected between 1991 and 2016 16. We used habitat selection models (Methods and 152 Supplement, Extended Data 1–3) of individual predat or species and then combined their spatial 153 predictions to identify regions important to our full suite of species (Fig. This enabled us to account 154 for incomplete tracking coverage (i.e., colonies from which no animals were tracked) and predict habitat 155 importance for each species across the entire Southern Ocean. Combined, these provided an 156 integrated and spatially explicit assessment of areas of high biodiversity and biomass at multiple trophic 157 levels. Sea surface temperature (SST) and wind strengt h were most often the best predictors of habitat 158 selectivity in these specie s-specific models (Extended Data 4). SST has been linked to global patterns 159 of marine biodiversity 18; in the Southern Ocean it acts as an indicator of water masses with different 160 ecological properties 19. Wind exerts several influences including driving ocean currents and mixing, 161 transport of iron, sea-ice dynamics, and determining primary production 20 and has been linked, for 162 example, to the global distri bution of albatrosses and petrels 21. The importance of other predictor 163 variables differed among species (Extended Data 4) .

The relationship between habitat selectivity and 164 environmental predictors differed across specie s showing how species used their environments in 165 different ways (Extended Data 5). 166 167 Distribution of Areas of Ecological Significance 168 Regions with the highest overall habitat importance scores were identified as Areas of Ecological 169 Significance (AES; calculated as the upper decile of those scores). These were located over the 170 Antarctic continental shelf (89% of AES pixels south of 60°S were over or within 200 km of the shelf) 171 and in two northerly aggregations: one encompassing much of the Scotia Sea and surrounding waters, 172 and the second covering the chain of sub-Antarctic islands from the Prince Edward Islands through to 173 parts of the Kerguelen Plateau (Fig. Regions of lower importance were identified in the southern 174 Pacific and Indian Oceans. The distribution of AES is associated with the availability of suitable 175 breeding/resting habitat, as well as regional oceanography and sea-ice dynamics that affect biological 176 production (Fig. The AES were based on a combination of island-breeding and wholly pelagic 177 species, and therefore reflect broad-scale patterns of importance. These patterns are supported by: (i) 178 broad-scale patterns of primary production — Southern Ocean land masses provide iron fertilization that 179 stimulates downstream production in this otherwise iron-limited ecosystem22; (ii) historical whaling 180 catches north of 60°S, which show that fewer whales were taken in the southern Indian or Pacific 181 Oceans, and that the region identified as an AES in the south Atlantic corresponds with high whale 182 catches23; and (iii) recent and historical estimates of Antarctic krill distribution, with high concentrations 183 in the south Atlantic and lower concentrations in the south Pacific and southern Indian Ocean24.

The 184 AES in the south Atlantic corresponds to the area of elevated krill biomass, whereas the AES in the 185 Indian Ocean partially corresponds to a region dominated by myctophid fish and other euphausiids25. 186 187 Exposure of Areas of Ecological Significance to potential stressors in the Southern Ocean 188 The Southern Ocean is subject to several stressors that influence its ecosystems, including expanding 189 resource extraction and rapid climate change26. We note that both temperature and wind, which were 190 important parameters in many of our species-specific habitat models, are changing and projected to 191 continue to do so27. 192 193 Fishing has both direct effects, through incidental bycatch, and indirect effects through resource 194 competition28. Many demersal finfish were exploited during the latter part of the 20th century, leading to 195 the decimation of some stocks in the Antarctic and sub-Antarctic5. Finfish fishing in the Antarctic is now 196 regulated and focused on toothfish species caught with longlines. Fisheries for Antarctic krill began in 197 the 1960s and are now concentrated in the south Atlantic sector, most notably at the Antarctic 198 Peninsula and South Shetland Islands, the South Orkney Islands and South Georgia6. Krill is managed 199 with a low, precautionary catch limit, taking account of the key role it plays in the Antarctic food web. By 200 global standards, fishing pressure in the Southern Ocean is low29, but indications are that pressure on 201 its marine resources will grow2,5,6.

Fishing effort (Fig. 2a) was significantly different inside and outside of 202 the AES (Fig. 2b), with a disproportionate amount of moderate-to-high effort (≥100 total hours of fishing) 203 occurring inside AES. Of cells with moderate-to-high fishing effort, 37.9% were AES, despite AES only 204 representing 10% of the study area. Areas of conspicuous fishing effort around southern South 205 America, New Zealand, and Australia should be treated with caution, since our study does not include 206 temperate predator species likely to figure prominently in these ecosystems (Fig. Nonetheless, 207 relatively high intensity fishing areas directly relevant to the Southern Ocean occurred around the 208 Falkland Islands/Islas Malvinas, where squid and some finfish are targeted, South Georgia (ice fish, krill 209 and toothfish), at the West Antarctic Peninsula (krill), and over the Kerguelen (toothfish and ice fish) and 210 Campbell (squid and finfish) plateaux4–6. Relatively important fisheries for toothfish also occur within the 211 Ross Sea30. 212 213 The physical attributes of the Southern Ocean ar e changing. Sea-ice is a critical component of high-214 latitude ecosystems, playing central roles in ocea nographic, biogeochemical, and ecological processes. 215 The biological consequences of sea-ice changes in the Southern Ocean include changes in breeding 216 site availability or access, prey availability, and changes to ecosystem structure and function 31.

The 217 pattern of change in sea-ice in the Antarctic displays considerable regional and temporal variation. In 218 the West Antarctic Peninsula, sea-ice extent has declined markedl y in recent decades, but has 219 increased in other areas 32. Most climate projections indicate that overall sea-ice will decline over the 220 next century27.

Given the broad influence of both SST and wind on ecosystems, these components can 221 also influence aspects of an animal’s biology, including breeding phenology, foraging success, survival 222 and reproductive performance26. However, when we contrasted the rates of change of sea-ice duration, 223 SST and wind patterns inside and outside of th e AES there were only slight differences, and 224 considerable regional variation (Extended Data 6). The subtle nature of the differences in environmental 225 change inside AES versus outside th em does not negate the fact that the study area, overall, is 226 undergoing marked changes in physical environmental processes, and that ecologically important areas 227 are not being spared from these changes. 228 229 Assessment of current and proposed spatial management 230 Management of marine systems is complex, especially in areas beyond national jurisdiction33 where 231 international effort is required, particularly for species that move between national and international 232 waters34. Relevant management includes traditional process-oriented tools, such as individual species 233 protection, stock assessments, decision rules and catch limits, as well as spatial tools such as marine 234 protected areas (MPAs)35, but also altered fishing practices for mitigating bycatch36. In the high-latitude 235 Southern Ocean, the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) 236 employs an ecosystem-based management framework intended to ensure that there are no long-term 237 effects from fisheries on marine ecosystems37.

This includes setting precautionary, spatially explicit 238 catch quotas and a call for the establishment of a network of MPAs, the design considerations of which 239 can include the potential to provide climate change refugia and the inclusion of reference areas to help 240 separate the effects of fishing from climate related environmental change. Both approaches will benefit 241 from better understanding of the locations of AES. Outside the CCAMLR framework, MPAs have also 242 been established by sovereign management authorities around some sub-Antarctic islands (Fig. 243 Several other MPAs are currently under development, including within CCAMLR and by national 244 authorities (Fig. However, the level of protection afforded by any individual MPA depends upon its 245 governance structure and the type and level of permitted activities (e.g., fishing)9,38 246 247 An appropriately designed protected-area network can help buffer the effects of climate change and 248 reduce the effect of stressors such as bycatch or competition from fisheries39.

We therefore quantified 249 the coverage and placement of individual MPAs with reference to identified AES. Overall, 7.1% of the 250 ocean south of 40°S is currently protected by MPAs, and this would increase to 11.2% if all currently 251 proposed MPAs were implemented (Fig. This already meets, in a regional setting, the 10% global 252 Aichi Target 11 for 2020. The Southern Ocean’s level of protection is high by global standards, as only 253 3.6% of the world’s oceans fall within MPAs, increasing to 7.3% with the addition of planned and 254 announced MPAs38. However, protection needs to be targeted at areas of high conservation value, 255 including those important for the persistence of biodiversity9. Existing MPAs cover 27% of the AES 256 identified (Fig. Southern Ocean MPAs are predominantly in sub-Antarctic regions, and here they 257 show high levels of congruence with AES (Fig. Of note is the Davis Bank region, south of the 258 Falkland Islands/Islas Malvinas, where there are high levels of fishing inside AES (Fig. This 259 area is now part of a recently implemented MPA by Argentina (Fig. Adoption of proposed MPAs for 260 the Antarctic continental margins would raise MPA coverage of AES to 39% (Fig. 3b), including areas in 261 East Antarctica, the Weddell Sea, and the Antarctic Peninsula. The largest total AES (4.0 million km2, 262 56% of AES) are under CCAMLR jurisdiction (Fig.

3a,c), followed by 1.9 million km2 (27% of AES) in 263 national waters (EEZs) and only 1.2 million km2 (16% of AES) are outside the CCAMLR Convention 264 Area and national waters (Fig. Implementation of MPA proposals would benefit Southern Ocean 265 ecosystems, especially those in the Antarctic Peninsula, East Antarctic and Weddell Sea. 266 267 Likely effects of future climate change 268 We estimated the likely effects of future climate change on the distribution of AES under two 269 Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) simulations: a medium-forcing scenario (RCP4.5) and a 270 more extreme, high-forcing scenario (RCP8.5)40. For each scenario, eight global climate models, 271 considered to be most suitable for Southern Ocean studies by reliably reproducing extant sea-ice 272 conditions, were used to predict locations of AES-like habitat in 2100. Here we discuss only the RCP8.5 273 results, since current CO2 emissions are in line with this scenario41. Results for the moderate RCP4.5 274 scenario are presented in Extended Data 7.

There was an overall reduction in AES-like area (-3.3%), 275 partitioned into an increase in sub-Antarctic AES-like cells (+5.7%), but outweighed by a decrease in 276 Antarctic AES-like cells (-10.2%). 277 278 In the sub-Antarctic, AES-like areas generally moved south (Fig. 4a), resulting in an overall growth in 279 sub-Antarctic AES area (Fig. This general southward migration of important habitat is consistent 280 with projections for individual predator species (e.g., 42) as well as for other species including krill and 281 salps43,44. The advantages for predators from the overall increase in area of sub-Antarctic AES may be 282 offset by increased cost of travel to more distant foraging grounds, at least for diving central place 283 foragers (penguins and fur seals), while volant species (albatrosses and petrels) or those unconstrained 284 by terrestrial breeding sites (whales) may benefit from increased sub-Antarctic foraging opportunities 285 (e.g., 45). Changes in the future distribution of AES-like areas along the Antarctic margin are more 286 spatially heterogeneous, with areas of AES loss interspersed with areas of AES gain or retention (Fig. However, there will be a net loss (-10.2%) of AES-like cells in the CCAMLR Convention area (Fig.

The heterogeneity of this pattern is due in part to the dynamic nature of the high-latitude Antarctic 289 marine environment and the uncertainty across a number of climate-model variables in this region. This 290 uncertainty is due to the variability in skill of models in reproducing current climate and the large 291 envelope of projected responses from those models. Our projections are based on unchanged future 292 availability (i.e., colony locations and sizes) and species-environment relationships. However, as 293 species adapt to future pressures and changes to available breeding habitat, populations are likely to 294 change both their preferred colony locations and habitat usage. Sub-Antarctic-breeding species have 295 limited availability of alternative breeding sites, but colony sizes might change. Ice-breeding species 296 may be able to relocate, whilst land-breeding species that require ice-free terrain may be able to occupy 297 previously vacant areas, or some may move to regions that become ice-free due to changing local 298 conditions (e.g., 46). Our projected loss of AES-like habitat on the Antarctic margin suggests that these 299 populations will be under pressure as the climate continues to change, and therefore continued 300 monitoring of these species, and on-going assessment of the effectiveness of management actions (e.g. 301 MPAs), will be important. Monitoring of colonies will need to detect local colonisations, particularly when 302 populations are small47.

As part of the designation of MPAs within CCAMLR, research and monitoring 303 plans are necessary and required; inter alia, these plans should consider changes to species-304 environment relationships and other dynamic processes within and adjacent to the protected area, given 305 the pressures of ongoing climate change. 306 307 There was a mixed response across the eight climate models, with changes in the number of AES-like 308 cells included in current MPAs ranging from -8.7% to +8.4% (Fig 4b). When the proposed MPAs are 309 included (current + proposed), all climate models indicated a decrease (between -16.9% to -0.9%) in the 310 number of AES-like cells within MPAs. This suggests that proposed MPAs are in areas projected to 311 become less-similar to existing AES by 2100. Any protection afforded by MPAs in such areas could 312 provide better medium-term opportunities for populations to adapt as they will not have to cope with 313 both climate change and other stressors during that period. 314 315 Conclusion 316 Our work provides strong evidence in support of the ecological importance of existing and proposed 317 Southern Ocean MPAs. By integrating tracking data from a suite of predators we identified regions likely 318 to have high biodiversity and biomass of the prey (and concomitant ecosystems) of the animals that 319 were tracked. Our AES are clearly candidates for protection; as such, the implementation of the 320 proposed MPAs within the CCAMLR region would greatly increase the protection of important Southern 321 Ocean habitat.

Several MPA proposals have failed to reach consensus within the CCAMLR process 322 and, even when adopted result in MPAs with varying degrees of protection. Many sources of input are 323 needed to establish MPAs, but the AES described here will play a key role in making the scientific case 324 in this multi-faceted process2,48, by providing ecosystem-level analysis of areas most warranting 325 protection. MPA design should also consider future conditions.

Pressures on AES due to climate 326 change will affect all parts of the Southern Ocean, but their effects are likely to be strongest along the 327 Antarctic margin. Species responses to these pressures are currently difficult to predict, highlighting the 328 importance of continued monitoring as part of ongoing management actions. Because only 16% of all 329 Southern Ocean AES lie outside the CCAMLR Convention Area or national waters, the responsibilities 330 for these future actions fall mostly to CCAMLR members and those nations with sovereign territory in 331 the sub-Antarctic.

Adaptive management approaches to conservation measures (including MPAs) will 332 be necessary to deal with these future changes in a timely way. The Southern Ocean can be an 333 exemplar of how science, policy and management can interact to meet the challenges of a changing 334 planet. In the Southern Ocean, these challenges will be considerable, including increased fishing 335 pressure as the global demand for marine resources grows49. Our results highlight where future 336 science-informed policy efforts might best be directed, including both adaptive spatial protection and 337 improved robust fisheries management. Similar synthetic approaches should capitalise on the 338 increasing amount of tracking data being collected through large-scale initiatives (e.g., 50) to indicate 339 regions in need of protection globally.

Nature 456 475, 86–90 (2011). 457 458 459 METHODS 460 Analytical overview 461 We assembled tracking data from 17 species of seabirds and marine mammals, collected between 462 1991 and 2016, from across the Antarctic predator research community16. Birds and mammals comprise 463 the majority of top predator species in the Southern Ocean, which has few other large, highly mobile 464 marine predator taxa (bony and cartilaginous fishes). These include toothfish, southern bluefin tuna 465 (Thunnus maccoyii, which occur in the northernmost part of our study area), and a small number of 466 shark species. Very few of these fish and shark species have been tracked, with very few tracking data 467 available south of 40°S51. However, this does not detract from the underlying logic of our approach: that 468 by using the at-sea distributions of an ecologically diverse suite of predators we can identify areas of 469 ecological importance. This benchmark dataset represents 4060 individual tracks and more than 2.9 470 million location estimates (Fig. After filtering and quality control, we retained 2823 tracks comprising 471 2.3 million locations16. The ~30% of tracks that were excluded were those with poor quality location fixes 472 that could not be properly filtered, tracks from individuals that did not actually depart the colony, or 473 tracks other problems detected during the rigorous quality control process that we implemented.

The full 474 process is described in our companion data paper16, which makes available all of the data for use by the 475 broader community, without providing further analytical investigation to consider the matters raised 476 here. The environmental covariate values along each of these tracks (the used habitat) were compared 477 statistically with the habitat available to each animal, thereby allowing each species’ habitat selection to 478 be determined (e.g., 52,53; see Extended Data 1 and 2). We fitted habitat selection models for different 479 life-history stages within a species. Despite the considerable size of the data set, it is not an exhaustive 480 representation of animals from all known colonies (for central-place foragers) or geographic regions (for 481 non-central-place foragers). To account for incomplete tracking coverage, we used the fitted habitat 482 selection models to map habitat importance for each life-history stage of each species across the entire 483 Southern Ocean, including areas around colonies without tracking deployments (Extended Data 3). For 484 each species we calculated the average habitat importance across life-history stages. For colony-485 breeding species, colony sizes were used to weight the habitat importance values, upweighting areas 486 important to large colonies (Extended Data 8). Southern Ocean predator species can be clustered into 487 Antarctic and sub-Antarctic species (Extended Data 9).

We mapped assemblage-level habitat 488 importance (Extended Data 10) for each of these two groups (hereafter “overall habitat importance” 489 maps) by averaging across species-level maps. To calculate the overall map, we took the maximum of 490 the two assemblage-level importance values in each cell. Areas with high values of overall habitat 491 importance (in the top decile of values) indicate areas that are attractive to many species; these 492 represent Areas of Ecological Significance17. We then compared the overall habitat importance values 493 inside and outside Areas of Ecological Significance in the context of fishing effort and changes in 494 physical environmental conditions (duration of sea-ice cover, sea surface temperature (SST) and wind 495 speed). We finally quantified the spatial protection afforded to Areas of Ecological Significance under 496 current and proposed spatial management plans. 497 498 We describe the methods in more detail in the Supplementary Information. We conducted all the 499 analyses in R54.

500 501 Tracking data 502 The data represent output from a variety of tracking tag types, providing location estimates at different 503 spatio-temporal resolution and accuracy. We applied a state-space model55 to estimate most probable 504 locations at regular temporal intervals while accounting for potential errors in the location estimates with 505 automatic and manual quality control before and after filtering16. While this procedure does not make the 506 track from a light-based tag as accurate as one from GPS device, it does provide a consistent 507 characterization of the positional accuracy across different tag types, allowing the uncertainty in position 508 to propagate into the uncertainty in the parameters of the fitted movement model and in the track 509 simulation step (see below). We further note that the light-based tag deployments were made almost 510 exclusively on sub-Antarctic animals (albatrosses and fur seals). The spatial scale of our results (Areas 511 of Ecological Significance) in the sub-Antarctic zone (~5 million km2) is considerably larger than the 512 likely scale of positional error of light-based tags (~100 km) and so we do not believe that using a 513 mixture of tag types has adversely affected our results.

514 515 Life-history stages 516 Most of the species in the study are central-place foragers (i.e., they return periodically to land or sea-517 ice to breed, moult or rest). The constraints faced by these predators at different stages in their life-518 history cycle mean that their movements differ markedly across these stages. We therefore fitted 519 models separately for up to five predefined life-history stages in each species’ breeding cycle. We 520 automatically assigned tracks to these stages based on calendar date, with manual reassignment where 521 necessary following examination of individual movement patterns. This resulted in 40 data subsets (17 522 species * 1–4 life-history stages) with sufficient data for habitat selection modelling (Supplementary 523 Information Table S1). 524 525 Simulating tracks to estimate available space 526 The observed locations only provide information about where animals occur, not about where they could 527 have gone. To estimate the geographic space potentially available to animals, we simulated sets of 528 tracks for each observed track. For each observed track, we simulated 50 tracks using the movement 529 model described above55. This yielded simulated tracks with movement characteristics (distributions of 530 step length and turning angle) that are the same as the observed track, but they are random and 531 independent of environmental effects.

Thus, the simulated tracks offer an estimate of the geographic 532 space that each animal could have occupied (given its movement characteristics and track length) if it 533 had no habitat preferences. The environmental differences between the available geographic space and 534 the utilized geographic space allow the habitat selection of the organisms to be estimated, as detailed 535 below. Locations at the animal’s home colony, and locations at known terrestrial resting sites, were fixed 536 at the corresponding time and date in the simulated tracks in order to accurately simulate central place 537 foraging behaviour (Supplementary Information). 538 539 Environmental data 540 To characterize the biophysical environment at observed and simulated locations, we compiled a suite 541 of 19 environmental covariates (Extended Data 2, Supplementary Information Table S2) and extracted 542 the value of these at each location. The covariates were remotely-sensed, measured in-situ or model-543 estimated and represent biophysical features that influence the movement, distribution and density of 544 marine predators (e.g., 52,53). It was not computationally feasible to temporally match environmental data 545 to each location estimate. Rather, we created a climatology spanning each tracking data subset 546 (species by life-history stage combination), using the predefined stage dates. We took the mean (or 547 standard deviation) of the environmental data that fell on these days of the year (stage dates) over the 548 whole study period (November 1991 to June 2016).

Some covariates (e.g., salinity difference) were only 549 available as monthly climatologies, and we used the months corresponding with the stage dates to 550 calculate the mean (or standard deviation). All covariates were resampled to a 0.1° x 0.1° grid; hereafter 551 we refer to the pixels of this grid as ‘cells’. We checked the covariates for each data subset for missing 552 values and if >10% of values were missing we excluded the covariate from that model. This influenced 553 mainly chlorophyll-a concentration, which was excluded from 17 of the 40 habitat models 554 (Supplementary Information Table S1). This affected life-history stages with a large proportion of winter 555 days, since chlorophyll-a data has poor winter satellite coverage due to being obscured by high cloud 556 cover. However, chlorophyll-a was rarely an important predictor in the models in which it was included; 557 thus, excluding chlorophyll-a from models probably had only a negligible effect.

558 559 Habitat selection models 560 We used a habitat selection modelling framework56 to model and predict the space use of marine birds 561 and mammals of the Southern Ocean. These models use the observed locations of each individual 562 animal and an estimate of the geographic space available to each individual, along with covariates that 563 characterize their environment. The environmental differences between the habitat that was utilized and 564 the habitat that was available allow the habitat selection of the organisms to be estimated. To fit the 565 models, we used boosted regression trees, a machine-learning algorithm that produces an ensemble of 566 regression trees that have been iteratively fitted in a boosting process to improve accuracy57. We tested 567 several other algorithms but boosted regression trees showed the best predictive performance in 568 another study53 and in our tests. For a given location, the response variable was whether the location 569 was an observed or simulated (available) location, and the explanatory covariates were the associated 570 environmental covariates. Boosted regression trees have four parameters that must be set: the number 571 of trees (boosting iterations), the maximum tree depth, the learning rate (shrinkage) and the minimum 572 number of observations in a node. We chose these values as the combination that minimised the area 573 under the receiver operating characteristic curve (a measure of model predictive performance) during 574 10-fold cross-validation.

We also used this metric to evaluate the final fitted models. We used the fitted 575 model to generate spatial predictions for the entire study region and we estimated the uncertainty 576 associated with these predictions using a bootstrap approach (Supplementary Information) 577 578 Accessibility model 579 The modelling procedure described above does not account for the accessibility of a given location to 580 an individual animal (in effect, it estimates the habitat selection of a given location in terms of its 581 environmental characteristics, but without considering whether or not the animal could actually reach 582 that location). For central-place foragers in particular, this is an important consideration.

We therefore 583 used a second set of models to account for this53. We modelled accessibility in terms of the number of 584 observed + simulated locations in a given cell as a function of that cell’s distance to the deployment 585 colony. We fitted binomial models with a smooth, monotonic decreasing constraint58, under the 586 assumption that the accessibility of cells should decrease with geographic distance. To estimate 587 uncertainty, we sampled curves from the posterior distribution of each fitted accessibility model to use in 588 a bootstrap approach (Supplementary Information). 589 590 We used these models to predict the accessibility of each cell over the study region to each species 591 during each life-history stage (that is, given the distance of a cell from a colony, the fitted accessibility 592 model provides an estimate of the probability that animals from that colony would be able to visit that 593 cell). For colony-breeding species (those other than humpback whales, crabeater and Weddell seals), 594 colony sizes were used to weight this accessibility estimate: for a given cell, the accessibility from all 595 known colonies of that species was calculated. A weighted mean of these accessibilities was then 596 taken, using colony sizes as weights. Thus, this weighted accessibility represents the probability that a 597 randomly-selected individual from the global population would be able to visit that cell, effectively 598 upweighting cells in the vicinity of large colonies.

599 600 For the non-colony breeding, ice-associated seals (crabeater and Weddell seals), we modelled 601 accessibility as a function of distance beyond the ice edge (15% ice concentration contour), rather than 602 distance to the colony. For humpback whales, we assumed that the whole study area was equally 603 accessible. 604 605 Habitat Importance 606 Transforming output and combining models 607 The habitat selection models predict the value of the habitat at a location given that the animals could 608 access that location. The predictions of the habitat selection models were therefore multiplied by the 609 predictions of the accessibility models to yield an index that reflects both the habitat selection of each 610 cell and its accessibility to the animals. This is not an estimate of the probability of a species using a 611 given cell, because that probability also depends on the prevalence of the species59. Since prevalence 612 varies between species, our habitat selection estimates cannot be compared directly between species. 613 We therefore partitioned the cells into decreasing percentiles based on area52 in order to obtain a 614 habitat importance map expressed in terms of area (e.g., cells with values of 90 or higher represent the 615 top 10% most important habitat by area for that species). We refer to this as habitat importance, and 616 these maps can be compared among species.

To create a single habitat importance layer for each 617 species, we averaged the stage-specific habitat importance layers. 618 619 Species grouping 620 We calculated community-level habitat importance by averaging species-specific habitat importance 621 maps. Sub-Antarctic regions are naturally more species-diverse than those of the Antarctic, and so a 622 simple average of all species together tended to strongly favour sub-Antarctic areas simply because of 623 their greater species diversity. To account for the differences in species richness between the Antarctic 624 and sub-Antarctic, we first defined two species groups using an Unweighted Pair Group Method with 625 Arithmetic Mean hierarchical clustering with Manhattan distance, applied to habitat importance scores 626 (Extended Data 9). This produced two clear groups: an Antarctic species group (emperor penguin, 627 crabeater seal, Antarctic petrel, Adélie penguin, Weddell seal) and a sub-Antarctic species group 628 (Antarctic fur seals, black-browed albatross, wandering albatross, sooty albatross, grey-headed 629 albatross, king penguin, macaroni/royal penguin, light-mantled albatross, white-chinned petrel). The 630 wide-ranging humpback whales and elephant seals did not clearly fall into either cluster, and so were 631 treated as belonging to both groups. The mean habitat importance was calculated for each of these 632 groups separately and then combined (Extended Data 10) by taking the maximum of the two values 633 (Antarctic and sub-Antarctic) in each pixel.

We refer to this final layer as the overall habitat importance. 634 635 Areas of Ecological Significance 636 To identify the most important areas, we calculated the 90th percentile (top decile) of the overall habitat 637 importance values. Cells with overall habitat importance values above this threshold together comprised 638 Areas of Ecological Significance. 639 640 Environmental pressures 641 To assess past environmental stressors on the Southern Ocean ecosystem, we calculated change in 642 SST, wind speed and sea-ice duration. We selected SST and wind because they were frequently the 643 most important predictor variables in the habitat models (Extended Data 4), and sea-ice concentration 644 since this was an important predictor for Antarctic species. Moreover, these variables are considered 645 important drivers of ocean and ecosystem dynamics (e.g., 18,60) and key axes on which environmental 646 change in the Southern Ocean has been detected (e.g., 26). For each cell, we calculated change in SST 647 (°C) or wind speed (m/s) as the difference between mean SST or wind speed in 1987–1999 and 2007–648 2017. For sea-ice duration, we calculated the difference in the mean number of days per year that each 649 pixel had a sea-ice concentration >15%, for the same periods. These periods represent the decades at 650 the beginning and end of a 30-year period covering our study period.

Thirty years is also the 651 recommended period for climate assessments61. We also obtained data on fishing effort, which is 652 considered to be a major environmental stressor in many regions of the Southern Ocean (e.g., 29,62) 653 from the Global Fishing Watch dataset, covering the period 2012–201629. We compared the values of 654 these four stressors in the Areas of Ecological Significance and outside cells using random permutation 655 tests with 10,000 permutations. The null hypothesis is that stressor values inside and outside Areas of 656 Ecological Significance are from the same distribution. 657 658 Future projections of Areas of Ecological Significance 659 Our predicted AES (under current environmental conditions) are determined by both the oceanographic 660 and climatic conditions of an area, as well as the accessibility of that area to each of our species of 661 interest. In principle it would be possible to use future projections of environmental data and 662 accessibility along with our fitted models in order to obtain future projections of AES. However, some 663 predictor variables are not available from the climate models used for the future projections, and while 664 other variables might appear to be available, they have different properties due to factors such as 665 different temporal and spatial resolution in the output, or the ability of the climate model to resolve the 666 relevant processes.

For example, sea surface height from satellite altimetry gives information about 667 frontal and mesoscale features. Yet, while sea surface height is available as an output from many 668 CMIP5 models, those models do not explicitly resolve mesoscale features63 and so the model-output 669 sea surface height data will not be acting as a proxy for the same oceanographic properties that 670 satellite-derived altimetry does. 671 672 To assess future distributions of AES-like habitat, we therefore used a k-nearest neighbour classifier 673 approach, conceptually similar to climate analogues (e.g., 64). For each grid cell we compiled current 674 (end of 20th century) environmental conditions, as well as projected conditions at the end of the 21st 675 century from climate models (see below). In terms of accessibility, most of our study species breed in 676 colonies, and “accessibility” for these species is determined by both the geographic distribution of their 677 colonies as well as the colony sizes. Currently, future projections of colony location and size do not exist 678 for our study species, although initial work has begun for some species (e.g., 46). Colony locations and 679 sizes were therefore assumed to remain constant, and so the accessibility of each grid cell to each 680 species was assumed to remain unchanged. For each grid cell, we compared its projected future 681 environmental and accessibility conditions to every cell in the current (20th century) grid and selected 682 the most similar five cells.

If the majority of those cells were from current AES areas, the projected cell 683 was labelled as “AES-like”, otherwise “not AES-like”. These projections therefore provide an indication 684 of the future distribution of AES-like environmental conditions, under the assumptions that colonies do 685 not move or change in size, and that the animals do not change their habitat preferences. These 686 assumptions are unlikely to hold in reality; however, examining the changes in AES-like habitat under 687 these assumptions allows us to isolate the effects of environmental change from colony or habitat-688 usage changes. As environmental change occurs, species are likely to adapt by changing their colony 689 distributions and habitat usage. The AES projections offer insights into the likely distribution of 690 environmental pressures, and thus where adaptation by species might be important. 691 692 Climate data were compiled from eight global climate models (ACCESS1.0, BCC-CSM1.1, CanESM2, 693 CMCC-CM, EC-EARTH, GISS-E2-H-CC, MIROC-ESM, and NorESM-M) considered to be most suitable 694 for Southern Ocean studies, by virtue of reliably reproducing extant sea-ice conditions65. These models 695 were from phase five of the World Climate Research Programme’s Coupled Model Intercomparison 696 Project (CMIP5). For each model, we extracted data for a 30-year period concomitant with our tracking 697 data (1976–2005), and for a thirty-year end-of-21st-century (2071–2100) period.

We extracted future 698 (2071–2100) climate data from projections under two Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 699 simulations: a medium-forcing scenario (RCP4.5, which assumes that society implements changes to 700 limit future CO2 emissions in the near future, with peak emissions occurring in 2040) and a more 701 extreme, high-forcing scenario (RCP8.5, which assumes little curbing of emissions and retains a strong 702 reliance on fossil fuels into the foreseeable future)40. Reference (1976-2005) data were extracted from 703 hindcast model runs that attempt to simulate historical conditions, and consequently use observed CO2 704 concentrations over the past 160 years to guide the models. 705 706 A maximum of eight variables were extracted for each model, depending on the available data (not all 707 models provide all variables), at monthly time resolution. The variables used were sea-ice 708 concentration, SST, sea surface salinity, sea surface height, the spatial gradient of sea surface height, 709 near-surface current speed, near-surface wind speed, and surface downward heat flux. The 30-year 710 mean and standard deviation of each variable was calculated over summer (December to February) 711 and winter (July to September) months. All variables were normalized to the range 0–1 prior to further 712 analysis. 713 714 The resulting set of up to 48 predictors (mean and SD of up to 8 environmental variables, each for 715 summer and winter, plus accessibility layers for 16 species) naturally showed high correlation between 716 many of the variables.

We used a principal components analysis to reduce the dimensionality of this 717 data set, choosing the lowest number of principal components required to explain at least 95% of the 718 variance in the original data; this number ranged from 14–17 components, depending on the model and 719 scenario. For each projected-climate cell, the nearest neighbours in the historical-climate grid were 720 calculated using Euclidean distance on these normalized and dimension-reduced data. 721 722 Animal Ethics Statement. 723 All work was conducted under the appropriate National or Institutional Ethics approvals.
